notes: Groceries: the state tax on food and food ingredients (0.125%) ended January 1, 2026 (Act 1008 of 2025); local sales taxes still apply. Candy and soft drinks are not food under Arkansas law (Act 141 of 2017) and stay taxed at the full 6.5%, which is not counted here.

Alcohol bought in stores: beer, wine and liquor bought in stores pay the sales tax plus an excise tax on the retail price remitted with it: 3% on wine and liquor and 1% on beer (rule GR-26). The 1% is counted on all of it; the further 2% on wine and liquor isn't, since no official figure gives their share of alcohol bought in stores (the 2022 Economic Census doesn't split liquor stores' sales by kind).

Drinks served pay the sales tax (by the bottle or by the drink). Restaurants and other mixed-drink permit holders also pay a 10% supplemental tax and an additional 4% on everything except beer and wine, counted here on drinks with distilled spirits, 43% of drinks served nationally (2022 Economic Census). Private clubs pay the 10% on beer and wine too, and some cities add a supplemental tax of their own on mixed drinks or at private clubs (Little Rock 10% on mixed drinks at restaurants, bars and hotels, and Fayetteville 5% on drinks other than beer and wine under 5% alcohol by weight, counted there; Conway 5% at private clubs, Ordinance O-11-54, and Springdale's supplemental beverage tax, not counted). Cities' advertising and promotion taxes on prepared food don't reach drinks served here: Little Rock's tax rate sheet says its tax does not apply to mixed drink sales, Conway's schedule and Jonesboro's guidelines apply theirs to food only, and Fayetteville's reaches only low-alcohol beer and wine (counted there); North Little Rock's code may reach drinks served at bars and clubs (not confirmed, not counted).
Barber and beauty services: not taxed (FTA 2017 survey answer).
Laundry and dry cleaning, and auto repair labor: taxed (FTA 2017 survey answer).

Motor fuel on which the state motor fuel tax is paid is exempt from sales tax. The per-gallon tax, left out here, is 24.7 cents for gasoline from October 1, 2026 to September 30, 2027 (unchanged; lower in border zones), plus a 0.3-cent environmental fee; a 2026 call to suspend it for 90 days was not taken up (reported).

Hotel and other short stays pay the sales tax plus the state's 2% tourism tax, and many cities add an advertising and promotion tax on lodging (Little Rock 4%, Russellville 3%); none of these is counted here (DFA rule GR-4; city pages).
Tobacco is assumed taxed at the general rate (excise taxes left out); not verified state by state.
gaps: Restaurant meals include the city advertising and promotion ("hamburger") tax on prepared food where the city or its A&P commission publishes the rate: Alma 1%, Bella Vista 1%, Benton 1.5%, Bentonville 1%, Cabot 1.5%, Camden 1%, Centerton 1%, Cherokee Village 2%, Conway 2%, Eureka Springs 3%, Fayetteville 2%, Harrison 1%, Hot Springs 3%, Jacksonville 2%, Jonesboro 2%, Little Rock 2%, Mena 1%, North Little Rock 3% (2% A&P and a 1% parks tax), Pine Bluff 2%, Searcy 1%, Sherwood 2%, Texarkana 2%, Van Buren 1%, West Memphis 3%. Other cities that levy one, or may (among them Lonoke, noted on its own page), have no rate confirmed from the city's own published sources yet, so their restaurant rates here leave it out; no state agency lists these taxes.

Arkansas's supplemental taxes on drinks served by mixed-drink permit holders (10% plus an additional 4% on everything except beer and wine; DFA rule GR-26) are counted on drinks with distilled spirits (the state notes give the share), and so are Little Rock's own 10% supplemental tax on mixed drinks and Fayetteville's 5% supplemental beverage tax. Private clubs pay the 10% on beer and wine too, and some cities tax drinks at private clubs (Conway 5%, Little Rock 5%); those are not counted, and which other cities levy a supplemental tax was not found (the official copy of the Arkansas Code sits behind a terms page). Cities' advertising and promotion taxes are counted on restaurant food only, not on drinks served: Little Rock's rate sheet says its tax does not apply to mixed drink sales and Conway's schedule applies its tax to food only (North Little Rock's code may reach drinks; not confirmed).

0500970: Alma's 1% advertising and promotion tax on prepared food and hotel stays is from the city's monthly A&P gross receipts tax report form (revised January 18, 2024); it is counted in the restaurant rate here.
0504030: Batesville's advertising and promotion tax is a 3% tax on lodging only, from March 1, 2017 (Ordinance 2017-01-01, in the city's ordinance archive); a 1% restaurant tax passed in 2005 (Ordinance 2005-6-1) was sent to a referendum (Ordinance 2005-9-1) whose result wasn't read, and no restaurant tax appears in the city's later ordinances, so none is counted in the restaurant rate here.
0505290: Benton's 1.5% advertising and promotion tax on prepared food and short-term lodging is the rate its A&P commission's site gives (the city runs the filing form, which shows the rate only once figures are entered); it is counted in the restaurant rate here.
0509460: Bryant levies no advertising and promotion tax: its code of ordinances has none (Municode, through January 2024), and Ordinance 2023-18 (3% on hotel stays, 1% on prepared food) failed at the special election of November 14, 2023, 195 for and 423 against (Saline County's official results). An earlier A&P tax of 2018 and 2019 was disbanded.
0515190: Conway's 2% advertising and promotion tax applies to prepared food only; its 5% beverage tax on drinks at private clubs isn't counted here, since private clubs' share of drinks served isn't known (City of Conway tax schedule, April 1, 2023).
0523290: Fayetteville's 2% hotel, motel and restaurant tax reaches only beer, wine and malt liquor under 5% alcohol by weight; other drinks served pay the city's 5% supplemental beverage tax instead (City of Fayetteville sales tax rates page). Both are counted in its rate for drinks served: 5% on drinks with spirits or wine (70% of drinks served nationally, 2022 Economic Census) and 2% on beer; stronger beer isn't separated.
0530460: Harrison's 1% covers prepared food and non-alcoholic drinks (Ordinance 944, as its advertising and tourism promotion commission publishes it); it is counted in the restaurant rate here.
0535710: Jonesboro's 2% tax covers prepared foods only (its A&P commission's Prepared Foods Tax Guidelines, under Ordinance ORD-21:046), so it isn't counted on drinks served.
0541000: Little Rock's 10% supplemental tax on mixed drinks at hotels, motels, restaurants and bars (5% at private clubs) is counted in its rate for drinks served, on drinks with distilled spirits (43% of drinks served nationally, 2022 Economic Census). Its 2% advertising and promotion tax applies to restaurant food, not to mixed drinks (City of Little Rock tax rate sheet).
0541420: Lonoke levies an advertising and promotion tax on food service (the city's 2020 business checklist and its A&P tax permit application); neither gives the rate, so none is counted in the restaurant rate here.
0547390: Mountain Home's advertising and promotion tax is a 2% tax on hotel and motel stays (Ordinance 2013-14, the commission's monthly report form on the city's page); it has none on restaurant meals.
0550450: North Little Rock's code (chapter 3, sections 1-3 and 1-4) levies its 2% advertising and promotion tax and 1% parks tax on the gross receipts of restaurants, bars and private clubs from prepared food and beverages, so they may reach drinks served; alcohol isn't named, and Little Rock says the same kind of tax doesn't reach mixed drinks there, so here they are counted on restaurant food only.
0553390: Paragould's advertising and promotion tax is a 3% tax on hotel, motel and short-term rental stays (City Code 38-71); its code levies none on restaurant meals.
0560410: Rogers' advertising and promotion tax is a 3% tax on hotel stays, from September 1, 2017 (Destination Rogers, its A&P commission); it has none on restaurant meals.
0561670: Russellville's advertising and promotion tax, as its city page describes it, is a 3% tax on hotel and motel stays (Ordinance 2077); no tax on restaurant meals is mentioned, so none is counted in the restaurant rate here.
0566080: Springdale's advertising and promotion tax is on lodging only (Code 2-136). Its code also has a supplemental beverage tax on drinks at hotels and restaurants (Code 6-34), whose rate and reach weren't read; it isn't counted here.

tiers.label: Arkansas incentive tier
tiers.publisher: Arkansas Economic Development Commission (Arkansas Department of Commerce)
tiers.what: Advantage Arkansas jobs income-tax credit is 1% / 2% / 3% / 4% of new payroll in Tier 1 / 2 / 3 / 4, with minimum new payroll of $125,000 / $100,000 / $75,000 / $50,000; Tax Back, Create Rebate (3.9% to 5% of payroll) and ArkPlus thresholds also ease from Tier 1 to Tier 4.

warn.text: Dermott may be flagged as a visitor economy only because the Census counts about one in eight of its homes as seasonal or vacation homes, which here are probably hunting camps rather than tourist rentals, so read that flag with care.

Hot Springs draws many visitors, but the area shown here isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes and its lodging places per resident fall under the flag's cutoffs, though 9 of its 14 census tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of Hot Springs's local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.
